output.title: Why subscription sprawl survives in small teams
output.body:
Subscription sprawl survives for the same reason a lot of back-office work survives: it stays just inconvenient enough to ignore. A tool gets added, the renewal note lands in someone’s inbox, and then the review gets buried under invoices, admin, and whatever is more urgent that day. The real problem is usually visibility, not the software itself.

For a small business owner, I would treat this as a workflow decision, not a cleanup project. The question is simple: can you list every active subscription and its renewal date right now? If you can’t, don’t start by automating. Do a one-time manual audit first so you have a clean list to work from.

If you can, the next decision is narrower: do you just need a spreadsheet and a quarterly review, or a small control that flags renewals before they happen? That kind of work fits Bareni’s model: one recurring workflow, a clear owner, and human approval still in charge for any cancellation or payment step. The build stays technical; the decision stays with you.

That is usually enough to stop subscription sprawl from hiding in plain sight. The first pass is unglamorous, which is often why it works.
